es.summary: La ICC es la incapacidad del corazón para bombear suficiente sangre oxigenada para satisfacer las demandas del organismo.
key_points: Disminución del gasto cardíaco por disfunción ventricular izquierda o derecha.
Retención de líquidos produce edema periférico y pulmonar.
BNP >100 pg/mL y fracción de eyección <40% confirman el diagnóstico.
Tratamiento de primera línea: IECA, betabloqueador y diurético de asa.
Control estricto de sodio (<2 g/día) y monitoreo de peso diario son esenciales.

pathophysiology: La disfunción ventricular reduce la fracción de eyección y el gasto cardíaco.
Aumento del volumen end-diastólico eleva la presión de llenado y provoca congestión.
Activación neurohormonal (RAAS, SNS) genera vasoconstricción y retención de sodio.
Retención de líquidos lleva a edema pulmonar y periférico.
risk_factors: Enfermedad coronaria y antecedentes de infarto.
Consumo excesivo de alcohol y tabaquismo.
signs_symptoms: Edema bilateral de tobillos y sacro.
Fatiga y disminución de la tolerancia a la actividad.
Tos seca, a veces con esputo rosado.
Aumento de peso rápido (>2 kg en una semana).
diagnostics: ECG: hipertrofia ventricular izquierda o arritmias.
Ecocardiograma: fracción de eyección <40% y dilatación ventricular.
Radiografía de tórax: cardiomegalia y líneas Kerley B.
Laboratorio: creatinina, electrolitos, hemoglobina; monitorizar función renal.
treatment: Betabloqueador (ej. carvedilol) para reducir la frecuencia cardíaca.
Diurético de asa (furosemida) para eliminar exceso de líquido.
Antagonista de aldosterona (espironolactona) en fase crónica.
Restricción de sodio (<2 g/día) y control de ingesta hídrica.
complications: Edema pulmonar agudo y síndrome de dificultad respiratoria.
Insuficiencia renal por bajo flujo renal.
Caquexia y pérdida de masa muscular.
nursing_care: Monitorear signos vitales, presión arterial, frecuencia cardíaca y saturación O₂ cada 4 h.
Registrar peso diario y balance hídrico estricto.
Auscultar campos pulmonares para detectar crepitantes.
Evaluar edema (pitting) y medir circunferencia de tobillos.
Administrar diuréticos según orden y observar respuesta urinaria.
Priorizar educación sobre dieta baja en sodio y adherencia a medicación.
patient_teaching: Tomar los medicamentos exactamente como se prescriben.
Limitar el consumo de sal a menos de 2 g al día y evitar alimentos procesados.
Controlar el peso diariamente; reportar aumento >2 kg en 24 h.
Realizar actividad física ligera (caminar 30 min) según tolerancia.
Reconocer signos de descompensación: disnea creciente, edema, tos con esputo rosado.

outcomes: Gasto cardíaco: mantener CO ≥ 5 L/min en 48 h

interventions.action: Evaluar signos vitales y saturación O₂ cada 4 h
interventions.rationale: Detectar deterioro hemodinámico temprano.

interventions.action: Administrar diurético de asa según prescripción y registrar volumen urinario
interventions.rationale: Reducir la sobrecarga de volumen y mejorar la perfusión.

interventions.action: Monitorear peso diario y balance hídrico
interventions.rationale: Identificar retención de líquidos antes de que se manifieste clínicamente.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre dieta baja en sodio y control de ingesta hídrica
interventions.rationale: Disminuir la activación del RAAS y la carga de trabajo del corazón.

interventions.action: Colaborar con el médico para iniciar o ajustar IECA y betabloqueador
interventions.rationale: Mejorar la contractilidad y reducir la postcarga.

care_plans.diagnosis: Riesgo de desequilibrio de volumen de líquidos
outcomes: Balance hídrico: mantener ingesta y salida de líquidos equilibradas en 24 h
Edema: ausencia de aumento de edema periférico durante la hospitalización

interventions.action: Registrar ingesta y salida de líquidos cada 8 h
interventions.rationale: Detectar desviaciones del balance y prevenir sobrecarga o déficit.

interventions.action: Evaluar edema (pitting) y circunferencia de extremidades diariamente
interventions.rationale: Monitorear la acumulación de líquido intersticial.

interventions.action: Ajustar restricción de sodio a <2 g/día y educar al paciente
interventions.rationale: Reducir la retención de agua mediada por el sodio.

interventions.action: Revisar resultados de laboratorio (electrolitos, creatinina) cada 48 h
interventions.rationale: Identificar desequilibrios que puedan requerir intervención.

interventions.action: Colaborar con el equipo para modificar la terapia diurética según respuesta clínica
interventions.rationale: Optimizar la eliminación de exceso de líquido sin causar hipovolemia.

en.summary: CHF is the inability of the heart to pump enough oxygenated blood to meet the body's demands.
key_points: Reduced cardiac output due to left or right ventricular dysfunction.
Fluid retention causes peripheral and pulmonary edema.
BNP >100 pg/mL and ejection fraction <40% confirm the diagnosis.
First‑line treatment: ACE inhibitor, beta‑blocker, and loop diuretic.
Strict sodium control (<2 g/day) and daily weight monitoring are essential.

pathophysiology: Ventricular dysfunction lowers ejection fraction and cardiac output.
Increased end‑diastolic volume raises filling pressure and causes congestion.
Neurohormonal activation (RAAS, SNS) induces vasoconstriction and sodium retention.
Fluid retention leads to pulmonary and peripheral edema.
risk_factors: Coronary artery disease and history of myocardial infarction.
signs_symptoms: Dry cough, sometimes with pink sputum.
Rapid weight gain (>2 kg in one week).
diagnostics: ECG: left ventricular hypertrophy or arrhythmias.
Echocardiogram: ejection fraction <40% and ventricular dilation.
Chest X‑ray: cardiomegaly and Kerley B lines.
Laboratory: creatinine, electrolytes, hemoglobin; monitor renal function.
treatment: ACE inhibitor (e.g., enalapril) to block RAAS.
Beta‑blocker (e.g., carvedilol) to reduce heart rate.
Loop diuretic (furosemide) to eliminate excess fluid.
Sodium restriction (<2 g/day) and fluid intake control.
complications: Acute pulmonary edema and respiratory distress syndrome.
Renal failure from low renal perfusion.
nursing_care: Monitor vital signs, blood pressure, heart rate, and O₂ saturation every 4 h.
Record daily weight and strict fluid balance.
Assess edema (pitting) and measure ankle circumference.
Administer diuretics as ordered and observe urine output.
Prioritize education on low‑sodium diet and medication adherence.
patient_teaching: Limit salt intake to less than 2 g per day and avoid processed foods.
Check weight daily; report an increase >2 kg in 24 h.
Engage in light physical activity (walk 30 min) as tolerated.
Recognize signs of decompensation: increasing dyspnea, edema, cough with pink sputum.

outcomes: Cardiac output: maintain CO ≥ 5 L/min within 48 h

interventions.action: Assess vital signs and O₂ saturation every 4 h
interventions.rationale: Detect early hemodynamic deterioration.

interventions.action: Administer loop diuretic as prescribed and record urine volume
interventions.rationale: Reduce volume overload and improve perfusion.

interventions.action: Monitor daily weight and fluid balance
interventions.rationale: Identify fluid retention before clinical manifestation.

interventions.action: Educate patient on low‑sodium diet and fluid intake control
interventions.rationale: Decrease RAAS activation and cardiac workload.

interventions.action: Collaborate with physician to initiate or adjust ACE inhibitor and beta‑blocker
interventions.rationale: Improve contractility and reduce afterload.

outcomes: Fluid balance: maintain intake and output equal within 24 h
Edema: no increase in peripheral edema during hospitalization

interventions.action: Record intake and output every 8 h
interventions.rationale: Detect deviations in balance and prevent overload or deficit.

interventions.action: Assess edema (pitting) and limb circumference daily
interventions.rationale: Monitor interstitial fluid accumulation.

interventions.action: Adjust sodium restriction to <2 g/day and educate patient
interventions.rationale: Reduce sodium‑mediated water retention.

interventions.action: Review laboratory results (electrolytes, creatinine) every 48 h
interventions.rationale: Identify imbalances that may require intervention.

interventions.action: Collaborate with team to modify diuretic therapy based on clinical response
interventions.rationale: Optimize excess fluid removal without causing hypovolemia.

summary.0.quote: Heart failure means that your heart can't pump enough oxygen-rich blood to meet your body's needs.

key_points.0.quote: Heart failure is a result of ventricular dysfunction; something has affected ventricular preload or contractility in such a way that the ventricle is no longer able to expel blood effectively (Malik et al., 2022).

key_points.1.quote: Diets high in sodium increase fluid retention, as water molecules follow sodium molecules into the vascular space and can leak into the interstitial tissue, creating edema.

sections.pathophysiology.3.quote: Fluid buildup and reduced blood flow to your organs can lead to serious problems, including: Breathing problems from fluid in and around your lungs (also called congestive heart failure)

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: The most common causes of HFrEF are coronary artery disease, acute myocardial infarction, and prolonged hypertension.

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: There are multiple causes of HFrEF, including coronary artery disease and acute myocardial infarction (AMI).

sections.risk_factors.4.quote: Both can cause heart failure exacerbations.

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: Patients may allude to difficulty sleeping due to struggles with breathing while lying flat, also called orthopnea .

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: Clients with heart failure often experience shortness of breath and fatigue with exercise; however, they should be encouraged to exercise as much as they are able.

sections.signs_symptoms.3.quote: Other assessment findings may be a frothy pink sputum or a productive wet cough.

sections.signs_symptoms.4.quote: Clients should notify their health care provider if they gain 2–3 pounds in one day or 5 pounds in one week or if they notice increased swelling in their extremities, difficulty breathing, and/or chest pain.

sections.diagnostics.2.quote: Normal levels of BNP should be less than 100 pg/mL, and may increase slightly due to age, but assessing levels along with the clinical presentations assists the nurse to evaluate the patient’s response to treatment.

sections.diagnostics.4.quote: Electrolyte panels assist with providing baseline serum potassium and serum and creatinine to consider if there is renal insufficiency.

sections.treatment.1.quote: Beta-blockers are utilized to reduce myocardial oxygen demand, vasodilate, and reduce heart rate.

sections.treatment.2.quote: Considered preload reducers, potent diuretics such as furosemide work on the loop of Henle and increase fluid excretion.

sections.treatment.5.quote: Putting the patient in high Fowlers will alleviate dyspnea, and ordered supplemental oxygen may be necessary to maintain oxygen saturations greater than 92 percent.

sections.nursing_care.1.quote: The patient’s response to diuretic therapy is monitored by daily weights, adhering to strict intake and output.

sections.nursing_care.2.quote: A lung assessment may reveal crackles in the pulmonary bases.

sections.nursing_care.4.quote: The patient’s response to diuretic therapy is monitored by daily weights, adhering to strict intake and output.

sections.nursing_care.5.quote: HF requires continued maintenance of medication adherence, modifiable risk factor management, and self-monitoring of disease.

sections.patient_teaching.0.quote: Take heart failure medications as prescribed by their health care provider.

sections.patient_teaching.4.quote: The classic presentation of HF includes lower extremity edema, weight gain, cough, sputum production, and alterations in hemodynamics.
